doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Being a woman in jazz
summary: Women's festivals gave exposure in the early 70s, but business acceptance has improved less than hoped.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well there’s a — I don’t know if it’s small or large, whatever — movement for women in jazz. Has it ever felt to you like you have been at a disadvantage or at an advantage because you were a woman playing jazz?
No easy answer to that question either, that’s a big one. There are both sides to the equation. When I began playing in the early 70s, there was a lot of consciousness in the

air about women’s issues. There were a lot of women’s jazz festivals that sprang up that I played at, and I got exposure through, that had they not been there I might not have been heard. But they were the one venue that I saw a possibility to play, and at that point in time I’d play anyplace, anywhere, anytime. So there was something beneficial about that environment at that time. Disadvantages? It’s been my point of view that things haven’t changed as much as I had hoped they would in 20 years. You know when I first started playing I thought things would be a lot better, the playing field would be a lot more equal than I see it today, and mostly in respect to the business environment of jazz. Because there are plenty of women players who are now out there, and they’re playing horns and they’re playing drums and bass, all the rhythm instruments, all the things that were not considered instruments for women to play in jazz, they’re out there playing them now. But the thing that kind of is upsetting is that when I talk to some of these younger women, I’m still hearing some of the same stories I remember listening to 20 years ago about social acceptance and business acceptance. So it has gotten better but boy, not as quickly and not as much as I had thought.
